w: Dr. Abou-Arraj taught this in two parts. He recorded the first part (posted Nov 9): gum thickness, receding gums and how they're grafted, missing firm gum, and the frenum. The last two problems, too much gum and gum discoloration, he taught in a live class on Nov 12, after answering questions on the recording; those answers are added where they belong. The class ended with his review for the final, which is in Exam Hints. The tissues The mucogingival junction (MGJ) is the line between the firm, pink gum (gingiva) and the loose, redder lining of the mouth (alveolar mucosa). You can often see it, but a probe finds it best. All the gum above that line is keratinized gingiva, the tough kind. Part of it is stuck down to the tooth and bone (attached gingiva); the edge is free (free gingiva), and that's where the probe slips in to measure pocket depth. Gum and lining problems Periodontal plastic therapy fixes mucogingival deformities: anything abnormal about the amount, size, outline or shape of the soft tissue around teeth. The current classification (the 2017 World Workshop) lists seven: (1) gum thickness and shape (the phenotype); (2) receding gums (recession); (3) not enough firm gum (lack of keratinized gingiva); (4) a shallow vestibule; (5) a frenum or muscle attached too high; (6) too much gum (gingival excess); and (7) discolored gum (a tattoo). Thin or thick gums The phenotype is how thick the gum is (thin or thick) and how its edge is shaped (scalloped or flat). To test thickness, put the probe in the pocket. If you can see the probe through the gum, it's thin, 1 mm or less. If you can't, it's thick, more than 1 mm. It matters because thin gum recedes more easily, and recession on thin gum tends to get worse; thick gum resists it. His example: a young patient with gum so thin you could see the roots was about to get braces. Braces plus years of brushing could make his gums recede, so before the braces the gum was made thicker: a flap was lifted, a piece of connective tissue from the palate was stitched over the two front teeth most at risk, and the flap was laid back over it. Two weeks later the gum was already thicker, and he went ahead with braces. Receding gums: what and who Recession means the gum edge has moved below the CEJ (where the enamel ends), so some root shows. Measure it from the gum edge to the CEJ at the same six spots as pocket depth. Check between the teeth too, because recession there changes what treatment can do. It's very common. The slide: 88% of people 65 and over and 50% of people 18 to 64 have at least one spot. In the recording: over half of Americans 30 and older have at least 1 mm, and almost a quarter have at least one spot of 3 mm or more. Older people have more because they've piled up more risk factors over the years, not because of age itself. It's more common in men and in African-Americans, and most common on the cheek side of upper molars (especially first molars) and lower front teeth; canines are common too. What sets it up The slide's list of ten: gum disease (periodontitis); injury (brushing, flossing, picking, objects); bone variations (a window or a gap in the bone over the root) and teeth out of line; not enough firm gum; thin gum; braces; past gum surgery; a frenum or muscle attached high; filling and crown edges; and chewing tobacco. What he added: Gum disease means periodontitis, not gingivitis: losing bone and attachment uncovers the root. Past gum surgery: resective surgery causes most of its recession on purpose, to leave no pockets, so the patient can keep the area clean. Brushing is the most common injury: hard bristles, or simply brushing too hard. Flossing habits, picking, objects like a fingernail or pen, and harsh medicines put right on the gum count too. Bone variations. A fenestration is a window in the bone over the root; a dehiscence is missing bone from the top edge down. A tooth that sits out toward the cheek has thinner gum and gets hit harder by the brush. Moving it back into line with braces can undo some recession without a graft. Thin gum plus missing bone plus hard brushing is "the perfect storm." Braces that push teeth out of their bone over thin gum can cause recession, though some studies disagree; he calls it controversial. Crown and filling edges placed under the gum, poorly fitting, or too bulky on thin gum can cause it (not that every crown needs a graft). A high frenum tugs on the gum edge with every movement. Chewing tobacco, held in one spot, usually the lower back teeth, can cause severe recession right there; his worst case had recession down to the bottom of the vestibule, with no pockets. How it happens Two ways. Brushing injury, especially on thin gum: the surface is scraped, the tissue underneath gets inflamed, a small sore forms, and with more injury the gum edge pulls back. Plaque: the same process as periodontitis, plaque left in the pocket causing attachment loss, just in one small spot on thin gum. Either way, his key word is inflammation: it's what actually causes recession. Everything on the list just sets it up. The Cairo grades: how much root can be covered? Before suggesting a graft, grade the recession, because the grade predicts the result. The Cairo system reads the attachment between the teeth. Attachment loss is the recession plus the pocket depth, measured in the middle between the teeth, not at the corner of the tooth. In healthy thin gum you probe about 1 mm on the front and about 2 mm between the teeth. (He doesn't plan to give you a chart and ask for numbers on the exam; expect general questions about the three types.) The three: RT1: no attachment lost between the teeth; you can't find the CEJ between the teeth. The best case: about 100% of the root can be covered. RT2: some attachment lost between the teeth, but no more than on the front of the tooth (the attachment loss between the teeth is less than or equal to the loss on the cheek side). You can see the CEJ between the teeth. Expect partial coverage, about 50 to 60% in his examples: only up to the level of the attachment between the teeth, because there's nothing there to hold the gum higher and no blood supply for it. His rule of thumb: on a tooth with more recession than its neighbors, no graft can cover past the gum line of the teeth next to it (the lower of the two). RT3: more attachment lost between the teeth than on the front. A graft won't cover the root at all, so don't try for coverage. The root itself gives a graft no blood supply; the graft lives on the bone and gum on either side, and in RT3 those sit too low. You might get thicker gum, but no coverage. To cover those roots, the answer is usually a filling or a crown. Why treat it Exposed roots and lost tissue make these more likely: (1) sensitive teeth, (2) sore gums (thin gum can hurt to brush), (3) root cavities, (4) looks, (5) harder cleaning, and (6) the gum inflames more easily. And it keeps going: a 2016 review (Chambrone and Tatakis) found untreated recession keeps getting worse. So "it doesn't hurt, let's just watch it" doesn't mean it will stay the same. Except for RT3, consider treating it when there's a reason to. (Fixing recession with fillings is next year's course.) Gum grafts: where they come from Two main sources: the patient's own tissue (an autograft) and donor tissue from a tissue bank (an allograft). Animal sources exist too. The most common graft comes from the palate, because palate tissue is the tough, keratinized kind, and its connective tissue teaches the new site to grow tough gum. Two kinds come from the palate: a free gingival graft (FGG), the surface layer plus the connective tissue in one piece; and a connective tissue graft (CTG), only the connective tissue, no surface layer. The palate's layers, from the surface down: a thin surface layer (0.3-0.6 mm), the thick connective tissue (1.25-3 mm), then fat and glands, then bone. A thick graft brings fat along, and that's trimmed off so it doesn't slow healing. Stay away from the big artery and nerve of the palate (the greater palatine). On the slide it sits about 7 mm from the CEJ in a shallow palate, 12 mm in an average one and 17 mm in a high one. So a high, deep palate gives the most room for error. Check how deep the palate is first: the shallower it is, the narrower the graft has to be. A CTG can be taken two ways: open a trap door and take the connective tissue from underneath, or cut out the whole piece with its surface layer and peel the surface layer off after. The exam-review guide's version: sometimes an FGG is cut but used as a CTG, because that's easier. The rule: if a flap will cover the graft, use connective tissue only, because surface layer pressed against the flap's underside won't heal. If the graft will be left uncovered, use an FGG. Or by the goal: to cover a root, the best is a CTG under a flap pulled up; to get more firm gum, an FGG. A CTG under the flap doesn't add firm gum on the surface (2 mm of firm gum before, about 2 mm after), but it covers the root and thickens the gum. An FGG can cover some root too, just less than a CTG on the same tooth. Covering a root: CTG under a flap pulled up His case: recession on #10 and #11. He lifted a flap, took a CTG from the palate, stitched it over the roots, and pulled the flap up over it (a coronally advanced flap), with no tension so it stays put. Four weeks later the roots were well covered, and the gum over them was much thicker, which resists more recession. His rule: "We always do a coronally advanced flap if we're trying to cover the graft." Many teeth: donor skin Grafting many teeth from the palate means a big, painful harvest. Instead, use an allograft: donated human skin (dermis), cleaned of its surface layer, hair follicles and cells, leaving a framework of collagen, elastic and reticular fibers. This is acellular dermal matrix (ADM), the most common donor graft (AlloDerm is one). It was made for burns and reconstructions (since 1995) and used in dentistry since 1997. Pros: no second wound on the palate, patients accept it more, shorter surgery, many teeth at once, good-looking results, easy to use. Cons: it's "more or less a dead piece of skin," like a band-aid, with nothing alive to help healing. So it must be completely covered by the flap; over time the body replaces it with its own tissue. In a tough site it can't match the patient's own tissue (the guide: it doesn't work as well as an autograft, but has many advantages). His case: five or six teeth, canine to canine, with RT2 and RT3 recession. He used a tunnel flap: like an envelope, but without lifting the gum between the teeth, joining the pockets of all the teeth into one tunnel under the gum. The ADM was soaked in two baths (the second with the antibiotic tetracycline), slid into the tunnel, held with sling stitches, and covered by pulling the flap up. Six months later it was a good result for that starting point. Not enough firm gum Keratinized gingiva (KG) is measured from the gum edge to the MGJ. To find the MGJ, look for the color change, or roll the probe up from the loose lining: the lining rolls with it, and where it stops rolling is the MGJ. On average the upper front teeth have the most, the canine and first premolar the least, and the molars more again; the lower arch is similar, and on the tongue side of the lower jaw the front teeth have the least. Do you need it? With good plaque control and no other injury, a band of attached gum isn't essential for healthy gums. But if plaque control isn't great, at least 2 mm of KG is needed to prevent attachment loss. Many patients don't clean perfectly, so a tooth with under 2 mm is likely to recede. Still, it's case by case: not every such tooth needs a graft. Growing firm gum: an FGG left uncovered His patient had RT2 recession, a sensitive tooth and no firm gum, so the spot trapped plaque and kept receding. The goal was a band of firm gum, with any root coverage a bonus. A CTG under a flap wouldn't help: the only tissue to cover it with was loose lining, and lining doesn't turn into firm gum by covering a graft. So he did an FGG: the flap was moved down (an apically positioned flap), and a graft with its surface layer was stitched on and left uncovered, so it heals into firm gum. The palate wound heals on its own (secondary intention). The graft is held only by stitches, so the patient shouldn't pull the lip to look at it, should eat soft food and shouldn't brush there while it heals. Three months later: a good band of firm gum, some root coverage (as expected for RT2), no more sensitivity, and a spot that's easier to clean. The frenum A frenum attached too high pulls on the gum edge every time the lip and face move, which traps plaque and makes recession worse. In one patient it was in the way of her new crowns looking good, so it was removed before the final crowns (a frenectomy): cut out the frenum in a diamond shape and close it with a few stitches into the lip. Too much gum Four causes, each with its fix. 1. Pseudopocket: swollen gums from gingivitis probe 4-5 mm and bleed, but there's no attachment loss and no bone loss. Fix: better home care, and a cleaning if there's tartar. It goes away. 2. Overgrowth from a drug, always on top of plaque gingivitis: seizure drugs (phenytoin is the best known), calcium channel blockers (blood pressure drugs, the ones you'll see most) and drugs that suppress the immune system (cyclosporine). A cleaning won't fix it, because the extra gum is tough and fibrous: it has to be cut away (gingivectomy), with a bur, a blade or a laser. You may also ask the patient's doctor about switching the drug. 3. Uneven gum lines between matching teeth: not a disease, but it bothers patients, and it's more common than drug overgrowth. Fix: gingivectomy or a flap moved down. 4. A gummy smile: showing a lot of gum when smiling. How much is too much depends a lot on the culture. Gummy smile: find the cause The causes: short teeth, because the crowns are naturally short or, more often, because the gum still covers part of them (altered passive eruption); an upper jaw that's too long (vertical maxillary excess), with normal teeth; a short upper lip or a lip that lifts too far; or a mix. The signs: odd tooth sizes and uneven gum lines (short teeth); a long lower third of the face (a long upper jaw); a lip under 20 mm (a short lip); a lip that lifts more than 8 mm. Gum that never moved down A tooth comes in until it meets the opposite tooth (active eruption). Then the gum slowly moves down to uncover the crown and settles near the CEJ (passive eruption). In altered passive eruption that last step doesn't happen, so teeth look short: the crown you see is shorter than the real one. It's graded two ways. Type 1: a wide band of gum, with the MGJ below the bone edge. Type 2: a normal band, with the MGJ at about the CEJ. A: the bone sits a normal 1.5-2 mm below the CEJ. B: the bone is within about 1 mm of the CEJ, or at it. Types 1A and 1B are the most common. In his examples, one patient was Type 2B: normal gum, short teeth, and the bone right at the CEJ of the front teeth. In another (Type 1), the central incisors were B and the laterals were A, so bone came off the centrals but not the laterals. Teeth in one smile can need different fixes. Before crown lengthening The crown you see (the clinical crown) versus all the enamel down to the CEJ (the anatomical crown). First a normal gum exam, because the gums must be healthy: pockets, plaque, bleeding, attachment loss and the width of firm gum. On the radiograph: where the bone is, the roots' length and shape, and no decay or infection at the root tip. Roots already shortened (by resorption or braces) limit how much you can lengthen. To find the bone, numb the patient and push the probe through to the bone (bone sounding); a 3D scan (CBCT) also works but isn't usually needed. Checking the smile Good photos help. Face symmetry: left against right, and the face's midline against the teeth's. The face in thirds: hairline to eyebrows, eyebrows to the base of the nose, base of the nose to the chin. The lower third should equal the middle third; a long lower third means the upper jaw is too long. The smile line: low shows no gum, medium shows up to 2-3 mm (ideal), high shows more. The edges of the front teeth should follow the lower lip. People who dislike their gummy smile learn to hide it, so get their real smile, not the posed one. The upper lip: 20-22 mm in women, 22-24 mm in men, and under 20 mm is short; it normally lifts 6-8 mm into a full smile, and more than 8 mm is too much. Inside the mouth: the gum line puts the central incisors and canines level (the canine up to 1 mm higher is OK) and the lateral incisors about 1 mm lower, toward the biting edge. Each tooth's gum peak sits slightly toward the back of the tooth (just distal of its middle). Tooth proportions: the golden proportion, so from the front, if the lateral is 1 wide, the central is about 1.6 and the visible canine about 0.6. A central incisor should be about 75-80% as wide as it is long (10 mm long, about 8 mm wide), never square. Odd proportions and uneven gum lines mean short teeth, usually from altered passive eruption. (Worn-down teeth are short for a different reason.) Treating a gummy smile By cause: short teeth (altered passive eruption): crown lengthening, plus fillings or veneers if needed; an upper jaw too long: lengthening teeth can't fix it (only so much crown can be shown before root), so jaw surgery with braces, maybe gum surgery at the end; a lip that lifts too far: Botox (repeated about every 6 months) or lip surgery, which comes back in close to half of patients (better with Botox too); a short upper lip: no good options (fillers can help a little), but it's not the usual cause. If there are several causes, combine treatments. Crown lengthening, type by type 1A, cut away gum (gingivectomy): there's extra gum and room above the bone for the gum's attachment, so the new gum line stays. 1B: cutting the gum alone doesn't last, because with the bone so close the gum grows back; instead, open a full flap and trim the bone to restore the normal distance higher up the root. Type 2: don't cut gum away, since the band is only normal width; always leave at least 2, ideally 3 mm of firm gum. Open a full flap and move the whole band down: in 2A without bone surgery, in 2B with it. Done right on a healthy patient, the bone surgery doesn't cause gum disease. Patient 1 A healthy 28-year-old woman with fluorosis who wanted veneers and didn't want braces. Her face thirds were equal (no long upper jaw), but she had a high smile line, flat gum lines on the front teeth, laterals higher than the centrals instead of lower, and square front teeth. Her right lateral had good proportions, so it became the reference tooth that didn't move. Matching the canines exactly would have exposed root, so the plan compromised there. A wax-up and a guide set the new gum lines. He trimmed the gum one tooth at a time, centrals first, then opened a full flap because the bone was at the CEJ, and removed as much bone as gum (2 mm for 2 mm) so the result stays put. Stitches came out at 1 week, temporary veneers went on at 3 weeks, and the final veneers waited 6 months for the gum and bone to settle; she's shown at 18 months. Discolored gum A gray tattoo in the gum usually comes from amalgam, from old root-tip surgeries (apicoectomies) that sealed the canal with it, which is no longer done. The fix: cut out the stained gum (a split-thickness, also called partial-thickness, preparation) and replace it with a free gingival graft from the palate, there just to replace the color. Three months later the graft's edge is smoothed (laser, blade or bur) so it blends in.
